title: Ampfield
text:
Type: Place
Name: Ampfield

Ampfield is a village in Hursley parish. At the instigation of Sir William Heathcote and the Rev. John Keble a new church, St. Mark, Ampfield, was built there, opened in 1841. It was on a slope in a pinewood, which struck them as very beautiful.

title: Church of the Resurrection, Eastleigh
text:
Type: Place
Name: Church of the Resurrection, Eastleigh

Built in 1868 with a donation of £500 from CMY. The architect was G. E. Street. It was destroyed by fire in 1985 and reconstructed as social housing flats in 2003.
See Tim Lambert, A Brief History of Eastleigh, Hampshire at www.localhistories.org/eastleigh
The Hampshire Advertiser (15 August 1868), 3, noted: The consecration of the Church of the Resurrection, Eastliegh, took place on Thursday, by the Bishop of Mauritius. The church has been erected principally by the liberality of Miss Yonge, of Otterbourne, and Mr. - Chamberlaine, of Eastleigh Parish, together with other contributors. The Rev. W. A. Longlands, of Eling, near Southampton, has been appointed incumbent. A choir of amateurs has been trained by Mr. Somerford, of Winchester Cathedral. . . The services were intoned, or read, by the Rev. W. A. Longlands, incumbent, the Rev. W. Harrison, Vicar, Eastmeon, the Ven. Archdeacon Jacob, of Winchester, the Rev. R. F. Wilson, &c.

title: About This Digital Edition
text:
This website was built using WordPress and in 2017 was moved to the Centre for 21st Century Humanities at the University of Newcastle, Australia. However, the original WordPress had customizations to its code that could not be reproduced in WordPress upgrades. The University of Newcastle archived this site as part of maintenance in 2025.



While the site was created in a legacy version of WordPress with customizations, the text could still be extracted from the database or the scrape of the website, for anyone interested in Yonge’s letters.
This modern edition has been migrated to Quarto, a scientific and technical publishing system, to ensure:

Long-term preservation - Uses standard markdown format
Future-proof technology - Based on open standards
Enhanced accessibility - Better mobile support and screen reader compatibility
Improved search - Full-text search capabilities
PDF generation - Can generate complete PDF archives
Sustainable maintenance - Easier to update and maintain




The migration process involved:

Database extraction - Extracting letters, person references, and metadata from the WordPress MySQL database
Content conversion - Converting WordPress HTML and custom annotations to standard markdown
Reference linking - Converting person and institutional references to proper hyperlinks
Footnote processing - Converting custom footnote system to standard markdown footnotes
Metadata preservation - Maintaining all original dating, location, and manuscript information



The original WordPress site used a custom annotation system:

[[person:ID]]Name - References to people mentioned in letters
[[other:ID]]Name - References to institutions, organizations, etc.
[[footnote:N]] - Editorial footnotes

These have been converted to standard markdown links and footnotes while preserving all the original scholarly apparatus.




All original metadata has been preserved, including:

Letter dates (both original and regularized)
Correspondent information

Manuscript locations and references
Editorial footnotes and commentary
Biographical data for referenced persons
Institutional information





Source Format: Quarto Markdown (.qmd)
Output Formats: HTML (website) and PDF
Search: Full-text search via Quarto
Hosting: Can be deployed to any static web host
Version Control: Source files can be managed with Git




For questions about this digital edition or to report issues, please contact the current maintainers.



The letters themselves are in the public domain. This digital edition respects the scholarly work of the original compilers while making the content more accessible and sustainable for future research.

title: Collection of British Authors
text:
Type: Topic
Name: Collection of British Authors

This was a series published by the Leipzig publisher Firma Tauchnitz, which circulated small paperback novels in English on the continent. Travellers were not meant to bring them back to England, because of the law of copyright, but of course many did. Many of CMY's works appeared in the series, and she received payments from Tauchnitz for many years.

title: Books for the Chicago Exhibition
text:
Type: Topic
Name: Books for the Chicago Exhibition

Alice Gordon had written to the Editor of The Times (5 January 1893): 'A library has been built in the Women's Building of the Chicago Exhibition, in which the best books written by women of all nations are to be exhibited. We are anxious that English women's writings should be well represented. A committee has been formed consisting of Miss Agnes Clerke, Mrs. W. K. Clifford, Mrs. Green, Miss Kingsley, Mrs. Humphry Ward, Miss Charlotte Yonge, and Mrs. J. E. H. Gordon, to collect a representative library.' She asked for the gift or loan of books or MSS.

title: Church restoration
text:
Type: Topic
Name: Church restoration

In Victorian England the question of the restoration of ancient churches involved several different considerations. Just as there was an immense amount of new church building, in which the Tractarians took an enthusiastic part, so there was also a great deal of church rebuilding. The Ecclesiological Society encouraged work which was Gothic, and supported on purist grounds the de-classicizing of many churches. Indeed it sometimes supported the removal of genuinely mediaeval work and its replacement by work which was consistent with the original period of the building. As well as this aesthetic and historicizing element, there was also a movement to open up churches to the poor, by removing the room-like pews rented by the gentry. And liturgical considerations meant that the Tractarians in some cases reinstated features of mediaeval churches, such as rood screens, which had been absent since the Reformation. CMY's sense of reverence meant that she refers to these issues only in passing in her fiction, for example when Clement pulls down the church's black mourning drapery in The Pillars of the House, although other novels, from the Rev. F. E. Paget's Milford Malvoisin (1842) to Thomas Hardy's Under the Greenwood Tree (1872), give a good idea of the ructions which these changes involved.

title: To Charlotte Anne Elizabeth Moberly
text:
Date: [dated by Coleridge after 1893]
From: Charlotte Mary Yonge
To: To Charlotte Anne Elizabeth Moberly
Manuscript location: MS location unknown. Printed in Coleridge, [[otherbook:40]Life] p. 325-326

My dear Annie- I can only be quite sure that Mr. Keble never taught me at my Confirmation anything about Fasting Communion. When he first came monthly celebrations began here at mid-day the last Sunday in the month, his idea then being that he would come over and assist. So Hursley was fortnightly mid-day first and last Sundays; Ampfield began on the third. Then it was begun at Hursley early on the intermediate Sundays, and I remember its being said that the poor women could come to it then. I am sure he never commended Fasting Communion to me, nor lamented the omission, though I have a dim idea that once when talking about the expedience of the presence of non-communicants, which he deprecated as a rule, he mentioned the wishing to fast as a possible reason with some, but I am not sure. Early celebrations were certainly never insisted on in this church in his time, but Mr. Wither’s refusal to me when I proposed it was after his death– I do not think it was thought of before. I cannot tell about his own practice, the only time I spent a Sunday at Hursley being when I was very young.Jimmy Young would know better. It is quite possible that his habits grew more strict as time went on, but I am quite sure he did not teach me to practise it, and that he deprecated the attendance without communicating as a rule (for I discussed it with him), only wishing for it for children as part of their immediate preparation for First Communion.- Your affectionate C. M. YONGE.

title: To Gertrude Mary Ireland Blackburne
text:
Date: Sept 24th [1897 or later?]
From: Charlotte Mary Yonge
From address: Elderfield Otterbourne
To: To Gertrude Mary Ireland Blackburne
Manuscript location: MS Charlotte Mitchell
My dear Miss Blackburne I have advised this Sister Margaret Paulu to write to you about her appeal, as you might manage to get it in for her. I did not know her Mother, they lived beyond our neighbourhood, but my father knew hers well in magistrate’s business, as Col A’Court, and had a great regard for him as an excellent person1
yours sincerely
C M Yonge

title: To the Reverend John Frederick Watkinson Bullock
text:
Date: Jan 31 [1894]
From: Charlotte Mary Yonge
From address: Elderfield Otterbourne
To: To the Reverend John Frederick Watkinson Bullock
Manuscript location: MS Bodleian Library, Oxford: MS English Letters: e.174 ff 165
Dear Mr Bullock, I think Gordon must have been confirmed, as he was chiefly brought up in England. I see you have marked Bishop Andrews.1 Can you tell me of any short biography of him, I have to recommend books for our Higher Religious Education Society - books for that era of James I
I doubt Miss C Coleridge having time to write for you. But Miss Anderson Morshead - Industrial School Andover - knew Bishop Gray well, and could write of him Could write of Abp Sancroft2 or Bp Mackenzie - whose sister Anne was one of truest saints I ever knew -
I think you should have Frances Havergal - She was most devout and good, though not High Church, but most attached to the church. Also Agnes - the devoted workhouse nurse, and I do think Mrs Trimmer and Hannah More ought not to be omitted. Also Lady Falkland3
I have a few doubts whether Miss Sellon realised this saintly ideal. However she fought a great battle
Yours truly
C M Yonge
Would Miss M Trench, the writer of Charles Lowder’s life write him for you?

title: To Christabel Rose Coleridge
text:
Date: Aug 21 [1899]
From: Charlotte Mary Yonge
From address: Elderfield
To: To Christabel Rose Coleridge
Manuscript location: MS Mrs Clare Roels/81
My dear C C F M P went on Saturday to various visits, before she goes, like an enterprising wandering woman to India. This is the upshot of our talks. She says I know nothing of the modern young woman, or what she likes or despises as old and goody, and she is in favour of a Phoenix, but not with the old name- and though she would have the substance of the China Cupboard &c go on, she thinks the playful names are despised, and would have answers by you and Bog Oak in your own names - (I can’t see this and said it was silly, but she holds that it is my being out of touch with the modern girl) Also she would I think not have it cheaper but I may be confused for I was tired and stupid and had too much to do on that Saturday- and of course we got discursive when we talked, but thinking it over, I fancy she knows more of the girls that fly about over the Continent than of home ones.1
But it is hard to keep up with both sides and the home, careful mothers diminish. And how are Church principles – now that we are not at the foundations as in the days of Catechism- to be done without controversy?
One thing she said, it should be written for men. Also that at some place where she had just been staying she found the public school boys did not read any ‘boys’ books’- not even Rudyard Kipling the Jungle book. I could not understand what they did read.
Sir W Besant’s letter is very kind and interesting. After all you will have to think of the man and his son who carried the donkey, and act on your own opinion. Miss Blackburne has written to Mary Morshead offering a temporary berth at the Churchwoman
Dear old Lady Hertford is beautiful and bright2
your affectionate
C M Yonge
Discussing modern doubtful books would upset the careful mothers – if there are any left. I see Besant says write for them – not FMP. I suppose the schoolroom girls are to be given up and left to St Nicolas and Girls Realm

title: To the Marchioness of Salisbury
text:
Date: April 4th 1899
From: Charlotte Mary Yonge
From address: Elderfield Otterbourne Winchester
To: To the Marchioness of Salisbury
Manuscript location: MS The Marquess of Salisbury, Hatfield House 3MCH/5/3/4
My dear Lady Salisbury I am venturing to ask if you would be so good as to present my niece Mrs Cromie at the coming drawing room. Her husband Captain Cromie has just been promoted from Morocco to Algeciras, and they are in England during the transit. It would of course be much more convenient to her to be presented now that she is at home than to have to come on purpose. If you have not to present her officially1 would you do so unofficially? And can you let her know at once that she may send in her name for the 10th or 16th of May. Her address is 6 Cornwall Terrace Regents Park NW I hope you are stronger2 and have escaped this spell of influenza
yours sincerely
C M Yonge

title: To the Marchioness of Salisbury
text:
Footnotes


In her capacity as wife of the Foreign Secretary. Captain Cromie was British consul in Algeciras. He himself was presented to the Duke of Connaught (The Times, 6 May 1899, 15) but we have not found a record of his wife's presentation. Although it was no doubt conventional for the wives of consuls to be presented at court, the fact that Cromie had divorced his first wife may have had some bearing on the issue, perhaps making it especially desirable that Joanna should appear under the aegis of someone at once so grand and so respectable as Lady Salisbury.↩︎
Lady Salisbury was ill and died on 20 November 1899.↩︎

title: Charlotte Yonge Scholarship, The
text:
Type: Topic
Name: Charlotte Yonge Scholarship, The

In 1898 fund-raising began to provide a University Scholarship from Winchester High School for Girls in honour of CMY. The appeal published in MP (April 1898) 469, in The Times (17 March 1898) 7, and elsewhere, signed ‘Esmé Stuart’, states ‘'The sum of £6000 will be required in order to found an Annual Scholarship of £50 to be held for three years'. Actually about £1800 was raised, less than had been hoped, and the first recipient, Amy Aubrey Locke, who was the daughter of the porter of Winchester College, was initially unable to take up the scholarship because it did not cover the entire expense. A presentation was made to CMY on 19 July 1899 in the school. According to the report in The Times (22 July 1899) those present included Amelie Leroy (‘Esmé Stuart’), the Rev. J. H. Merriott, the hon. treasurer of the committee, Miss Mowbray, the Sumners, the Hon. Mrs Joyce, Mrs Harold Browne, Christabel Coleridge, Eleanor Price and Mrs Anderson Morshead. The scholarship continued to be awarded at least until the 1930s.

title: 70th Birthday Presentation to CMY
text:
Type: Topic
Name: 70th Birthday Presentation to CMY

The presentation of an autograph album to CMY on her seventieth birthday, which was organized by the Moberly family, is described by Coleridge, Life, 281-2, and Battiscombe, Charlotte Mary Yonge, 159.
The following report appeared in The Times (16 August 1893), 8:
'The 70th birthday of Miss Yonge has been marked by a presentation to her from admirers in all parts of the world. An album containing 5.000 autographs and criticisms of her writings was left on her birthday at her dwelling in the village of Otterbourne. On the front page is the following inscription in an illuminated border:- "Charlotte Mary Yonge - We offer our hearty congratulations on your 70th birthday, and desire to express to you the great enjoyment we have received from your writings, and our belief that they have done much good in this generation. August 11, 1893." Amongst the signatures are those of the Archbishop of York, the Earl of Selborne, the Marquis of Salisbury, Viscount Wolmer, the Bishops of London, Manchester, Salisbury, Chester, Bath and Wells, Chichester, Leicester, Reading, Southwell, Cape Town, Connecticut, and St. Helena, Bishops Selwyn, Jenner and Hobhouse, the Deans of Winchester, Windsor and Salisbury, Canon Scott Holland, the Warden of Keble College, Mr. Balfour and several members of Mr. Gladstone's family, besides the local clergy and gentry. The Queen of Italy sent a large photograph of herself, bearing her autograph and accompanied by a congratulatory note. Local presentations were made to Miss Yonge on the eve of her birthday.'

title: The Letters of Charlotte Mary Yonge
text: Welcome to the digital collection of the correspondence of Charlotte Mary Yonge (1823-1901), English novelist, historian, and educator.

title: The Letters of Charlotte Mary Yonge
text:
About Charlotte Mary Yonge
Charlotte Mary Yonge was a prolific English novelist, best known for her family saga The Heir of Redclyffe (1853) and her large family of children’s books. She wrote over 160 works, including novels, textbooks, and historical works, most of them for a Christian audience.

title: The Letters of Charlotte Mary Yonge
text:
About This Collection
This website contains 1,918 letters from Charlotte Mary Yonge’s correspondence, originally compiled and digitized by the Centre for 21st Century Humanities at the University of Newcastle, Australia. The letters span her lifetime and provide insight into Victorian literary culture, education, and religious life.

Features

Searchable Letters: Browse and search through all letters by date, correspondent, or content
Person References: Biographical information about people mentioned in the letters
Book References: Information about Charlotte Mary Yonge’s published works
Institutional References: Information about organizations, societies, and institutions mentioned

title: Atalanta
text:
Type: Periodical
Name: Atalanta

This was a magazine for girls (1887-1896), edited until 1893 by L. T. Meade, which CMY considered populist and trivial in comparison with the Monthly Packet. She contributed to it ‘John Keble’ Atalanta (May 1888) 466-71. A conciliatory letter from Meade to CMY (MS Mrs Clare Roels, 4 September 1889) is evidently a reply to one in which CMY had complained of the ‘want of definite religion’ in the magazine.

title: All Saints' Church, Hursley
text:
Type: Place
Name: All Saints' Church, Hursley

The parish church of Hursley was substantially rebuilt in 1847-8 to the designs of William Harrison, under the supervision of the Rev. John Keble, and partly funded from the profits of his bestselling volume of poetry The Christian Year. CMY describes the fittings of the interior and the symbolism of the stained glass in some detail in John Keble's Parishes (1898), 115-124. She emphasises that the work coincided with the Tractarian crisis following Newman's secession, so that the reconstruction was an act of faith at a time of great anxiety and doubt, while the movement was the target of vilification and suspicion. She enumerates the gifts made by Keble's friends and supporters to beautify the building, and no doubt they symbolize among other things the dependence placed on him at that time.

title: Hursley
text:
Type: Place
Name: Hursley

At the time of CMY's birth the village she lived in, Otterbourne, was ecclesiastically part of the neighbouring parish of Hursley, where the principal landowner, Sir William Heathcote, Bt., lived at Hursley Park. In her teenage years the Vicar of Hursley, the Rev. John Keble, in collaboration with Heathcote and CMY's father, was engaged in a programme of church and school building, which eventually led to the creation of the new parishes of Ampfield and Otterbourne out of Hursley.
